newsitem.title: USA: Stocks and bonds tumble on new inflation worries.
newsitem.headline: Stocks and bonds tumble on new inflation worries.

text.p: Stock and bond prices tumbled to a sharply lower close on Tuesday after new economic data revived the market's inflation fears.
The dollar fell against the German mark, while corn prices rallied after the U.S. Department of Agriculture cut its estimate for this year's harvest.
The Dow Jones industrial average staggered lower, ending below 8,000 points for the first time in three weeks on new evidence that economic growth is accelerating from its tame second quarter pace.

The Dow slumped 101.27 points, or 1.2 percent, to 7,960.84. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,549 to 1,252 on moderate volume of 499 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The economic news, which came in the form of a stronger than expected weekly report on the nation's retail sales, dealt a severe blow to the already jittery bond market.
The Redbook retail sales index showed seasonally adjusted retail sales rose a robust 0.9 percent in the week ended Aug. 9.
Analysts said the weekly Redbook figures renewed inflation fears in a market already on edge ahead of Wednesday's release of a critical monthly retail sales report.

"People are aware of the potency of (tomorrow's) retail sales number," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "If there's any sign the consumer is really starting to spend, that will push the whole inflation issue right back to the forefront," he added.

In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slumped 13/32, or $4.06 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.67 percent from 6.64 percent at Monday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Investors were also awaiting Wednesday's producer price index for July, and there was concern that the inflation gauge may rise after falling for six straight months.
"To dismiss PPI out of hand would be a mistake," said Pat Alexander, head trader at BancAmerica Securities. "But retail sales is clearly what the market is more focused on."
With stocks still richly valued and investors back on their heels, analysts predicted more volatility for the near term.
"We're in a nervous environment, and volatility is a fact of life here," said James Crawford, senior vice president at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc.
"I wouldn't be surprised by a period of consolidation here, and ultimately I think it's probably going to prove to be beneficial over the long term," he added.

The dollar slipped against the German mark Tuesday amid renewed fears the Bundesbank might raise interest rates next week to strengthen its battered currency. The dollar closed at 1.8630 marks, down from 1.8640 Monday, but rose to 116.28 Japanese yen, up from 116.18 on Monday.
Elsewhere, corn prices soared on Tuesday after the Agriculture Department cut nearly a half-billion bushels off its estimate of this year's crop.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn futures for delivery in December closed 12 cents higher, their maximum daily increase, at $2.65-1/4.
Overseas, Britain's FTSE 100 closed at 5,075.8, up 43.9 points, or 0.87 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-stock Nikkei average closed at 19.099.11, up 274.93 points, or 1.46 percent.
